summary: Saint Kitts and Nevis is a twin-island country in the eastern Caribbean, the smallest sovereign state in the Western Hemisphere by area and population, which became independent from Britain in 1983.

ranking.name: Anglican
ranking.description: After the English colonized Saint Kitts in 1623, the Church of England (Anglican Church) came with them and became the colony's official church, with a parish system covering the whole island. Because it long represented the colonial government and the planter class, its influence among the enslaved was actually less than that of Methodism, but it is still one of the largest single denominations today.

ranking.name: Methodism
ranking.description: In 1787 Thomas Coke, a colleague of the founder of Methodism, John Wesley, arrived in Saint Kitts, and Methodist missionaries preached among the enslaved, emphasizing personal faith and equality, attracting large numbers of Black believers. Many villages in Nevis and Saint Kitts center on the Methodist church.

ranking.name: Pentecostalism
ranking.description: Pentecostalism was introduced in the mid to late 20th century from the United States and other Caribbean countries, emphasizing experience of the Holy Spirit, praying in tongues and fervent styles of worship, attracting many young people and working-class people, and is one of the fastest-growing denominations in recent decades.

ranking.name: Seventh-day Adventist
ranking.description: The Seventh-day Adventist Church was brought to the Caribbean by American missionaries in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, distinguished by observing the Saturday Sabbath and valuing healthy diet and education; it runs schools in Saint Kitts and Nevis, and its membership has steadily grown.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: After British colonization in 1623, Catholicism was long restricted, since British colonies treated Anglicanism as orthodox. Only after the 19th century was the Catholic Church gradually established there, with believers including some descendants of Irish and Portuguese (Madeiran) immigrants, as well as recent immigrants from other Caribbean countries.

ranking.name: Moravian Church
ranking.description: The Moravian Church originated in what is now the Czech region and was one of the first Protestant groups to preach to Caribbean slaves, arriving in Saint Kitts in 1777. They set up schools among the enslaved and taught reading and writing, with a profound influence on the religion and education of the Black community, and several long-established churches remain today.

religion.background: In 1623 Britain established its first British colony in the Caribbean on the island of Saint Kitts, and the Anglican Church came with the colonists and was long the state church, serving mainly white planters. From the 18th century Moravian (1777) and Methodist (1787) missionaries began preaching to enslaved Africans and providing them with literacy education, and the two denominations thus grew rapidly in the Black community. After abolition in 1834, these churches became the heart of the community. From the 20th century Pentecostal and Seventh-day Adventist churches introduced from the United States also expanded rapidly, making the religious landscape more diverse.

ranking.name: Saint Kitts Creole English
ranking.description: The West African slaves brought to the sugar plantations in the 17th–18th centuries came from different ethnic groups and could communicate only on a base of English vocabulary, blending the sounds and syntax of West African languages, which formed Saint Kitts Creole. It is the language used by the vast majority of residents at home and among friends, and the accent on Nevis differs slightly.

ranking.name: English
ranking.description: English has been the administrative language since British colonization in 1623 and remained the sole official language after independence in 1983, with standard English used in schools, government, courts and the media. Most residents can switch between Creole and standard English according to the occasion.

language.history: The English in 1623 and the French in 1625 each colonized the island of Saint Kitts, and after the Treaty of Utrecht in 1713 the whole island went to Britain. Planters imported large numbers of slaves from West Africa to grow sugarcane, and the slaves developed Saint Kitts Creole English by blending the grammar of West African languages with English vocabulary. English is the language of the colonial government, churches and schools, and remained the sole official language after independence in 1983. Creole is widely used in daily life, but was long regarded as an informal language.

ranking.name: Saltfish (salted cod)
ranking.description: Salted cod soaked to remove the salt is stewed and sauteed with onion, tomato, sweet pepper and herbs, and is often combined with breadfruit, spicy plantain and coconut dumplings to make the national dish.
ranking.history: Salted cod is a product of the colonial-era Atlantic triangular trade: Newfoundland and New England in North America shipped cheap salted cod to the Caribbean as rations for slaves, in exchange for sugar and molasses. The islands produce no cod, yet saltfish thus became central to the local diet. Today stewed saltfish with breadfruit and plantain is designated the national dish of Saint Kitts and Nevis, commonly seen at Sunday breakfast and festivals.

ranking.name: Breadfruit
ranking.description: Breadfruit can be roasted, boiled or fried, or seasoned with spices and butter and made into a savory side dish. It has a potato-like texture and is rich in starch, and is often used as a staple.
ranking.history: Breadfruit is native to the Pacific. In 1793, on his second voyage, the British captain William Bligh (the protagonist of the "Bounty" affair) carried breadfruit saplings from Tahiti to St Vincent and Jamaica in the Caribbean, with the aim of providing cheap food for plantation slaves. Breadfruit then spread across the West Indies, becoming an important source of starch in Saint Kitts and a component of the national dish.

ranking.name: Spicy plantain
ranking.description: Ripe plantain is cut into pieces, seasoned with chili, spices and a little sugar, then fried or stewed, sweet with a touch of heat. Crisp outside and soft inside, it is often one of the side dishes of the national dish.
ranking.history: The plantain is native to Southeast Asia and spread to the Americas via Africa in the 15th–16th centuries, becoming an important food of Caribbean plantations during the slave trade. Caribbean people like to season with the local Scotch bonnet pepper, forming a spicy style. It is one of the side dishes of the national dish and also often appears at family lunches.

ranking.name: Goat water
ranking.description: A thick soup stewed from goat meat, flour dumplings, vegetables such as papaya, and spices, with the aroma of tomato and clove. The broth is rich and spicy, and it is often eaten with bread or rice.
ranking.history: Goat water is regarded as another national dish of Saint Kitts and Nevis; the name looks simple, but it is in fact a very thick stewed goat soup. It originates in the tradition of the enslaved and the free cooking nourishing soups from cheap, easily raised goats, influenced by both Irish stew and African stews. Today at carnivals, cricket matches, elections and community gatherings, people often cook goat water in big pots to share.

ranking.name: Conkie
ranking.description: A sweet cake made from cornmeal, pumpkin, sweet potato, coconut, spices and sugar, wrapped in banana leaves and steamed. It is soft, chewy and sweet, with the aroma of coconut and spices.
ranking.history: Conkie is generally thought to originate in the cornmeal cakes of West Africa wrapped in banana or corn leaves and steamed (such as Ghana's kenkey), and after being brought to the Caribbean through the slave trade it came to be made with local pumpkin, sweet potato and coconut. In the colonial period it was a sweet that plantation slaves could eat only at festivals; today it is linked in the eastern Caribbean islands with celebrations such as Independence Day and carnivals, and in Saint Kitts and Nevis it is also a traditional treat at family gatherings.
